newsitem.title: USA: Republicans head for clash with Clinton on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Republicans head for clash with Clinton on taxes.

text.p: Soundly defeated by President Clinton over flood relief last week, Republicans seem to be heading for a new confrontation with the White House over tax cuts in the budget.

The president, boosted by a strong economy, seems to be in no mood for compromise. Last week he made it clear he would not accept the budget bills coming out of Republican-run tax committees of Congress.
"We're not going to tax people who work and this new tax proposal ... would penalise the working poor and especially working poor mothers," Clinton said Friday.

So far, neither he nor anyone else at the White House has uttered the word "veto," which might even revive the possibility of another government shutdown in the autumn if spending bills are not passed in time. But White House spokesman Mike McCurry did say the tax legislation in its current form had no chance of becoming law.
Clinton is clearly emboldened by his victory on flood relief, where he forced Republicans to strip unrelated provisions that he found objectionable from the bill.

The measure that emerged last week from the House Ways and Means Committee would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years and includes a child tax credit that would give families a $400 tax credit in 1998 for each child under age 17, increased to $500 in following years.

But the bill also includes cuts in the capital gains tax for individuals and corporations and in the estate tax that Democrats believe would overwhelmingly favour the rich. The Senate is working on similar provisions.

"Two-thirds of the tax benefits go to 20 percent of the people in the highest income brackets. And we also show that 90 percent of it goes to people making over $100,000," said New York Representative Charles Rangel, the panel's senior Democrat.

Committee Chairman Bill Archer said Clinton's idea was to fritter away tax relief on welfare. "What the president wants to do is to take money away from middle-income Americans with teenage children and give it to an increase in welfare spending. And that's not what we're about," he said Sunday.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, under fire from his own troops and from conservative commentators for mishandling the flood relief debacle, seems intent on a new test of strength with Clinton.

"I really think the president is not committed to giving working Americans, middle-class Americans, a tax cut. I think they're getting positioned to veto the tax cut provision," Lott said Sunday on ABC's This Week.
"So beginning Monday, we're going on the offensive in trying to explain what's in the bill, why it's important to working Americans, and what the president is up to," he said.

To former White House adviser George Stephanopoulos, Lott seemed to be about to embark on another suicidal charge against Clinton's entrenched guns. "It seems like they've learned the wrong lessons from it all over again, and they're going to go down the same exact road with this tax bill, which is skewed toward the wealthy. And they're going to run into a buzz saw," Stephanopoulos said on the same show.

One problem is that Republicans themselves are far from united. Some dissidents in the House have circulated an unsigned memorandum citing "blunders" by the leadership and calling for a confidence vote.

"The economy is rolling along, politics and policies are centre-right and President Clinton is stealing the right's best lines: smaller, government, lower taxes, traditional family values," Lawrence Kudlow, chief economist for American Skandia Life Assurance Corp., wrote in the ultra-conservative Washington Times.
"Nearly all conservative thinkers and critics are cranky, angry, resentful, frustrated, dejected, pessimistic and declinist," Kudlow wrote.
The conservatives hardly sound like a group fired up for a new clash with a president who has repeatedly outmanoeuvred his political foes.
